message.content:
**Hydrogen – A Quick Reference Guide**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | H‑1 (protium, 99.98 %), H‑2 (deuterium, 0.02 %), H‑3 (tritium, trace) |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV (first) |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV (negative, so H⁻ is unstable in vacuum) |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Polarizability | 0.666 Å³ |
| **Physical Properties (STP)** | State | Gas |
| | Color | Colorless |
| | Odor | Odorless |
| | Taste | Tasteless |
| | Density | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (≈0.00008988 g cm⁻³) |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) |
| | Specific heat (gas, 1 bar) | 14.304 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Heat of vaporization | 0.425 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Speed of sound | 1270 m s⁻¹ (at 20 °C) |
| | Refractive index | 1.000132 (at 589 nm) |
| **Chemical Properties** | Bond type | Diatomic (H₂) – covalent, single bond |
| | Bond dissociation energy | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Reactivity | Highly reactive; forms hydrides with metals, acids, and many nonmetals |
| | Oxidation states | +1 (most common), –1 (rare, e.g., LiH) |
| | Acid–base behavior | Acts as a weak acid (HF) and weak base (H₂O) in aqueous solution |
| | Combustion | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (exothermic, ΔH ≈ –286 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Hydrogen bonding | H₂O, HF, NH₃, etc. – key for water’s high boiling point, acidity, etc. |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Protium (¹H) | Stable, most abundant |
| | Deuterium (²H) | Stable, heavier, used in NMR, D₂O (“heavy water”) |
| | Tritium (³H) | Radioactive (β⁻ decay, t½ ≈ 12.32 y), used in fusion research and radiolabeling |
| **Nuclear Properties** | Nuclear spin | ½ (protium), 0 (deuterium), ½ (tritium) |
| | Magnetic moment | 2.7928 µ_N (protium), 0 (deuterium), 1.0665 µ_N (tritium) |
| | Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) | ¹H NMR is the most widely used spectroscopic technique |
| **Astrophysical & Energy Applications** | Stellar fusion | 4 p → ⁴He + 2 e⁺ + 2 ν_e (pp chain) |
| | Fusion research | D–T fusion (D + T → ⁴He + n + 17.6 MeV) |
| | Space propulsion | Hydrogen fuel cells, cryogenic rocket propellants |
| | Environmental impact | Clean combustion (water vapor only) – potential for green energy |
| **Miscellaneous** | Solubility in water | 1.6 g L⁻¹ at 25 °C (low) |
| | Solubility in organic solvents | Variable; often used as a solvent in gas-phase reactions |
| | Safety | Extremely flammable; forms explosive mixtures with air (4–75 % H₂) |
| | Detection | Flame test (blue flame), gas detectors (electrochemical, infrared) |

---

### Quick Takeaways

1. **Hydrogen is the simplest element** – one proton, one electron, and (in most cases) one neutron.
2. **It exists mainly as a diatomic gas (H₂)** under normal conditions, but it can form a wide variety of compounds (hydrides, acids, organics).
3. **Its isotopes have distinct roles**: protium is ubiquitous, deuterium is a key tracer and in heavy water, tritium is radioactive and central to fusion research.
4. **Hydrogen bonding** is a defining feature of many of its compounds, especially water, influencing boiling points, acidity, and many biological processes.
5. **In energy and astrophysics**, hydrogen is the fuel of stars and a candidate for clean, high‑energy fuels on Earth.

Feel free to ask for deeper dives into any of these categories—whether you want the quantum mechanical details of the H₂ bond, the thermodynamics of hydrogen combustion, or the role of hydrogen in planetary atmospheres!
